chapter: Postwar records, Miami and Los Angeles
title: Adding the conga to the band
summary: The Miami band had Vidal Bolado on conga from late 1944; Machito says the conga is the second bass of the rhythm section.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: In the - while you were down Miami Beach that year, what was the number of men in your band?
Well, we had three trumpets, four saxes, a complete rhythm section, bongo, conga, timbales ....
You already had a conga at that time, before Chano came here?
Ah, yes. Vidal Bolado, he left the band to go with Stan Kenton. Vidal Bolado was the conga player.....
Yeah, that was 1947.
No, no, I mean when he went to Kenton, it was '47.
'47, so he played two years with us.....
Ah - Ha
.... as a matter of fact, he started in La Conga, 1944, late '44, with us and we took Vidal Bolado, our conga player, to Miami where there was Mangual, Vidal, Uba, Andino and Rene Hernandez.
Okay, so then that's the first time you had a conga.
Right.
Forty-four? Okay, and who were your trumpet players?
There was Bobby Woodlen.
Was Doc Cheatham in the band Yet?
No.
He already left?
No, Bobby Woodlen took Doc Cheatham place.
Okay, what made you put a conga in the band?
Because we need more bass, we need more - something to hold the rhythm better, not depend alone on the bass, so actually the conga is the second bass of the rhythm section.
I see. Had you heard about Arsenio
introduction of the conga into the dance band?

Well, I know that before Arsenio Rodriguez had his band. Is a lot of things that you don't recall. How could you, I mean it's like a person in the United States that doesn't register and vote. Are you recognized by a Democrat or a Republican as a voter? You are not registered, you are no voter; so recording became the last word of your life, I mean, to be accepted or whatever.
